hampi.title: As Large as Rome. Then Tigers Moved In. 🐅
hampi.desc:
In 1520 a Portuguese visitor said Vijayanagara looked as large as Rome. Less than fifty years later, travellers reported tigers living in its empty houses. This is how Hampi fell.

In January 1565, near Talikota, the Vijayanagara army faced a coalition of the Deccan sultanates. Its leader, Rama Raya, was captured and killed, the army collapsed, and the capital was looted and burned for about five months. The royal court never returned. Today the ruins of Hampi are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

rome.title: Rome Complained India Was Draining Its Money 💰
rome.desc:
Around 77 CE the Roman writer Pliny the Elder complained that India took at least 50 million sesterces from the empire every year, for pearls, fine cloth and above all pepper from Kerala. Roman ships rode the monsoon winds from Egypt to the port of Muziris. A Tamil Sangam poem remembers the Yavana ships arriving with gold and leaving with pepper, and a papyrus cargo list shows one ship, the Hermapollon, carrying goods worth about seven million sesterces. Roman coin hoards are still being found across South India.

Sources:
- Pliny the Elder, Natural History 6.101 and 12.84
- Akananuru 149 (Sangam poem on the Yavana ships at Muciri)
- The Muziris Papyrus (P. Vindob. G 40822), Austrian National Library; L. Casson, "New Light on Maritime Loans: P. Vindob G 40822" (1990)
- F. De Romanis, "The Indo-Roman Pepper Trade and the Muziris Papyrus" (Oxford, 2020)
- Kerala Council for Historical Research, Pattanam excavations
- R. Krishnamurthy, "Late Roman Copper Coins from South India"; P. J. Turner, "Roman Coins from India" (1989)

amaravati.title: Burned for Lime: India's Lost Buddhist Wonder 🏛️
amaravati.desc:
The Great Stupa of Amaravati, on the Krishna river in Andhra Pradesh, was one of the greatest Buddhist monuments of ancient India, faced with carved white limestone panels. It was not destroyed by war. In 1797 the surveyor Colin Mackenzie recorded it, but a local zamindar had already begun digging the mound for building stone. When Mackenzie returned in 1816 much of it was gone: slabs reused in buildings, others burned in kilns for lime. In 1845 Walter Elliot dug again and sent sculptures to Madras, where they stood in the open for years before many were shipped to London. Today more than 120 are in the British Museum, the Government Museum in Chennai holds the largest collection, and at Amaravati itself only a low mound remains.

Sources:
- British Museum: "The Amaravati sculptures" (collection and gallery notes)
- Robert Knox, "Amaravati: Buddhist Sculpture from the Great Stupa" (British Museum Press, 1992)
- Archaeological Survey of India: Amaravati site and museum
- Government Museum, Chennai: Amaravati gallery
- James Fergusson, "Tree and Serpent Worship" (1868), on the Elliot marbles in Madras
